subject: music
source_note: Topic structure follows the Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Music specification. Connections, sequence and prerequisites are expert-authored teaching relationships.

units.blurb: Composition to a brief and free composition

units.name: Appraising
units.blurb: Listening across the four areas of study

topics.name: Solo Performance
topics.blurb: Performing as a soloist on voice or an instrument

topics.name: Ensemble Performance
topics.blurb: Performing as part of an ensemble

topics.name: Composition to a Brief
topics.blurb: Responding to a WJEC-set brief and its conventions

topics.name: Free Composition
topics.blurb: Composing freely to develop a personal style

topics.name: AoS1: Musical Forms & Devices
topics.blurb: Binary, ternary, rondo, variation, strophic; Baroque/Classical/Romantic

topics.name: AoS2: Music for Ensemble
topics.blurb: Texture and sonority in jazz/blues, musical theatre, chamber music

topics.name: AoS3: Film Music
topics.blurb: Scoring mood and atmosphere for film and television

topics.name: AoS4: Popular Music
topics.blurb: Idioms and conventions across popular music genres

connections.why: Forms and devices from the Western Classical Tradition model the structures set in the WJEC brief
Knowledge of forms gives a framework for shaping free compositions
Skills learned writing to a brief transfer to free composition
Studying ensemble textures directly supports performing within an ensemble
Ensemble repertoire is built from the same forms and devices studied in AoS1
Film scoring techniques for mood and atmosphere feed original composition
Popular song is a common context for solo performance
Band and pop textures are typical ensemble performance settings
Both rely on modern, often amplified instrumentation and production
Solo control of an instrument underpins playing within an ensemble
Knowing an instrument's idioms helps write idiomatic original music
Performing repertoire deepens understanding of musical forms and devices
